plain_summary: The endpoint that lists employees always pulls every employee record out of the database at once, because nothing tells it to fetch one page at a time. On a small test dataset it looks fine, but as the number of employees grows each request gets slower and uses more of the application's memory, until enough simultaneous requests can exhaust it and stop the service responding.
summary: EmployeeService.getAllEmployees() (src/main/java/com/example/migrationdemo/service/EmployeeService.java:46-52) calls the inherited, no-argument JpaRepository.findAll() and streams the result into a List<EmployeeResponse>. No Pageable, Limit, Sort or filter argument is passed, so the query has no bound: the size of the result set is decided by how many rows the employees table holds, not by what the caller asked for. The method is reached by exactly one path, EmployeeController.getAllEmployees() behind GET /api/v1/employees, and that handler declares no page or size request parameter, so a caller cannot bound the read voluntarily either. Two full copies of the dataset (List<Employee> plus List<EmployeeResponse>) are live on the heap at the same time for the duration of every request.
expected_flow: Caller requests one page of employees
Heap use stays flat as data grows

root_cause.statement: getAllEmployees() invokes the unbounded no-argument findAll() overload instead of a paginated findAll(Pageable), so the query carries no result limit and the response size is governed by table size rather than by the API contract.
root_cause.explanation: The method body is `return employeeRepository.findAll().stream().map(employeeMapper::toResponse).collect(Collectors.toList());` (EmployeeService.java:46-52). EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long> (src/main/java/com/example/migrationdemo/repository/EmployeeRepository.java:15) and declares no override of findAll, so the call binds to the inherited zero-argument overload, which issues a select over the employees table with no LIMIT. The evidence bundle records findAll() as the only collaborator call this method makes, resolved against the injected EmployeeRepository field and marked as inherited from a framework base type with no method node of its own. Because .stream().map(...).collect(...) is eager, the returned List<Employee> is fully materialised before the mapped List<EmployeeResponse> is built, so both lists are retained simultaneously. The graph shows a single reaching path, EmployeeController.getAllEmployees() to EmployeeService.getAllEmployees() (1 upstream caller path, 0 downstream callee paths), exposed as GET /api/v1/employees on the spring-boot-migration-demo module. The handler signature ResponseEntity<List<EmployeeResponse>> getAllEmployees() (EmployeeController.java:31-35) takes no parameters at all, so no page, size or limit can be supplied by the caller. That is the mechanism behind the reported symptom: latency, response size and heap footprint all scale linearly with row count, with no ceiling anywhere on the path.

causal_chain.detail: An authenticated caller issues GET /api/v1/employees, which Spring dispatches to EmployeeController.getAllEmployees() (EmployeeController.java:31-35); the handler accepts no page or size parameter, so the request carries no bound.
The handler calls employeeService.getAllEmployees() with no arguments, which is the only outgoing call edge from this handler in the graph.
EmployeeService.getAllEmployees() calls employeeRepository.findAll() (EmployeeService.java:48) with no Pageable or Limit, so Hibernate emits an unrestricted select over the employees table.
Every row is hydrated into a List<Employee>, then eagerly mapped into a second full-size List<EmployeeResponse>, so two complete copies of the dataset sit on the heap at once.

Because nothing on the path caps the result, footprint and latency grow linearly with table size and multiply by the number of concurrent callers, degrading the instance and eventually exhausting the heap.

contributing_factors: No pagination convention exists on the REST surface: none of the seven endpoints listed in the architecture document declares a page or size request parameter, so unbounded list returns are the house style rather than an oversight at one site.

The three other read methods on EmployeeService - searchByDepartment (line 100), findActiveEmployeesByDepartment (line 108) and findHighEarners (line 116) - each return an uncapped List<EmployeeResponse> from a filtered query, so the same shape is already replicated and is the pattern a new endpoint would copy.

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto is set to update and the default datasource is a local H2 file (src/main/resources/application.yml:5-13), so development and test runs exercise a small dataset where the defect is invisible.
No existing test asserts a bounded result size for the list endpoint, so growth in row count cannot fail the build.

impact.narrative: The affected area computed by the collector is a single module, spring-boot-migration-demo, two types (EmployeeController and EmployeeService) and one endpoint, GET /api/v1/employees. No scheduled job reaches the defect site, and the only graph fan-in to EmployeeService is EmployeeController. Within that area the consequence is availability rather than confidentiality: every call to the list endpoint reads the entire employees table and holds two full copies of it on the heap for the life of the request, so response time, payload size and memory pressure all grow with the dataset and multiply across concurrent callers. Because the application runs as a single Spring Boot instance over one datasource, a small number of simultaneous calls against a large table is enough to drive sustained GC and then an OutOfMemoryError, which takes down every other endpoint sharing that JVM, including the create, update and delete paths. The endpoint is behind HTTP Basic authentication (SecurityConfig.java:33 requires authentication on /api/**), so triggering it requires valid credentials in this workspace; it is not an anonymous denial-of-service primitive here.
impact.severity_rationale: High is defensible on availability grounds: the failure mode takes the whole application down rather than degrading one feature, it is deterministic, and it worsens silently as production data accumulates. It is not Critical in this workspace, because the endpoint requires authentication and the result is projected into EmployeeResponse rather than returning the persistence entity, so there is no accompanying anonymous or over-broad data exposure at this call site.

recommended_fix.approach: Give the read an explicit bound at the query rather than after it. Change EmployeeService.getAllEmployees() to accept a Pageable and call the findAll(Pageable) overload, returning Page<EmployeeResponse>, and let EmployeeController.getAllEmployees() bind that Pageable from the request. This addresses the cause - a query with no limit - rather than the symptom, because the LIMIT and OFFSET are then pushed into SQL and the JVM never holds more than one page regardless of table size. Cap the page size in configuration so an oversized size parameter cannot restore the original behaviour.

changes.change: Change getAllEmployees() to getAllEmployees(Pageable pageable), call employeeRepository.findAll(pageable), and return Page<EmployeeResponse> via .map(employeeMapper::toResponse) so the mapping stays on the page rather than on a materialised full list.
Change the GET /api/v1/employees handler to accept a Pageable argument with a default page size and return ResponseEntity<Page<EmployeeResponse>>, so the API contract states the bound explicitly.
Add spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size and spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size so the server, not the caller, owns the ceiling.

verification: Add a service or repository test that persists more rows than the default page size and asserts getAllEmployees(PageRequest.of(0, 20)) returns exactly 20 elements with the correct totalElements - this test fails against the current unbounded implementation and passes after the fix.
Keep org.hibernate.SQL at DEBUG (already set in application.yml) and confirm the statement emitted for GET /api/v1/employees now carries a limit and offset clause where it previously had none.
Replay GET /api/v1/employees against a seeded dataset and assert the response is a page object whose content array length equals the requested size rather than the full row count.
Confirm an oversized request such as GET /api/v1/employees?size=100000 is clamped to the configured max-page-size instead of being honoured.
Run the existing EmployeeControllerTest and EmployeeServiceTest suites, updating only the assertions that expect a bare List body, to confirm no other behaviour changed.
Load-test the endpoint concurrently against a large employees table and confirm peak heap is flat with respect to row count.
prevention: Adopt a repository convention that any method returning a collection either takes a Pageable or carries an explicit Limit, and treat a bare findAll() inside a @Service as a review blocker.
Set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size globally so no endpoint can be talked into an unbounded read through a query parameter.
Add an ArchUnit or static-analysis rule that fails the build when a @Service method calls the zero-argument findAll() overload.
Seed integration tests with a dataset larger than one page so unbounded reads surface in CI rather than in production.
open_questions: Three of the five affected_symbols in the register do not exist in this workspace and could not be resolved against artifacts.json: EmployeeReportServiceImpl.getEmployees, WomenDaySchedulerImpl.printWomenDayMessage and EmployeeReportController.exportToExcel. Paths 2 (the Women's Day scheduled job) and 3 (the XLSX payroll export) described in the issue could therefore not be checked here at all - this diagnosis covers only the call site corresponding to the issue's Path 1.

The two symbols that did resolve, EmployeeSchedulerServiceImpl.getAllEmployees and EmployeeSchedulerController.getAllEmployees, matched only through the collector's last-resort method-name fallback: neither EmployeeSchedulerServiceImpl nor EmployeeSchedulerController exists in this workspace. They landed on EmployeeService.getAllEmployees() and EmployeeController.getAllEmployees(), which do exhibit the reported unbounded-read defect, but the register's symbol names should be corrected to the real ones by whoever filed the issue.

The issue describes a MongoDB collection read through a Spring Data Mongo repository. This workspace has no MongoDB dependency at all; it is JPA and Hibernate over H2 or PostgreSQL, and EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository. The unbounded-read mechanism is equivalent, but the Mongo-specific remarks in the issue do not apply here.

The issue states the entity is serialised directly, exposing address and phone number. That is not the case at this call site: the result is projected into EmployeeResponse, and the Employee entity declares no address or phoneNo field. The data-exposure sub-claim of the issue is not reproduced here, although EmployeeResponse does still carry salary.

The heap-exhaustion threshold is not established by static evidence. The proportional relationship between row count and footprint is proven from the source, but the row count at which the instance actually fails needs runtime confirmation against production-like data and a known JVM heap size.

The issue's reproduction steps assume an anonymous caller against ports 8502 and 8503. In this workspace the application serves port 8080 and GET /api/v1/employees requires HTTP Basic authentication, so reproduction needs credentials; whether the deployed configuration matches SecurityConfig was not verified at runtime.
